p = "docs/security.md"
s = open(p).read()

anchor = "## Data residency"
new = """## Column classification from your warehouse

DataQ masks failing-row samples by default and surfaces only what it can justify
showing (#415). The strongest justification available is **your own governance**:
if a column is classified in the warehouse, DataQ reads that classification and
treats it as the floor — a suite-level setting cannot lift it.

### The convention

A **fixed, documented convention**, not a per-connection mapping. A mapping would
be more flexible and worse: every deployment would express the same idea
differently, the mapping itself would become an unreviewed security control, and a
typo in it would silently un-mask a column.

Tag your **columns** with the key **`dataq_classification`** (matched
case-insensitively):

| Value | Effect |
|---|---|
| `sensitive` · `pii` · `confidential` · `restricted` · `secret` | **Always masked.** A suite policy cannot show it |
| `public` · `non_sensitive` · `nonsensitive` | Cleared — may be shown, unless the value itself is affirmatively personal data |
| anything else | **Ignored**, exactly as if untagged — see below |

**Snowflake additionally honours its own `PRIVACY_CATEGORY`**, set by Snowflake's
built-in classification. Its values (`IDENTIFIER`, `QUASI_IDENTIFIER`,
`SENSITIVE`) all mean personal data, so all three mask. It has no clearing side:
Snowflake omits the tag for data it does not consider personal rather than marking
it public, so an unexpected value means *unknown*, not *safe*.

**An unrecognised value is ignored rather than guessed at.** Guessing has only two
directions, and one of them un-masks data. `internal` is the worked example: it
sounds like a classification and is commonly the default stamp on everything, so
reading it as a clearance would clear whole tables in exactly the organisations
careful enough to tag them.

### Where it applies

Only **Snowflake** and **Unity Catalog** have a column-tag concept. ADLS, S3,
Iceberg and flat files have no authoritative source to read, so for those the
classification remains the suite's own policy, the name/value classifier, and
fail-closed mode. This is a limit of the platforms, not a gap in the
implementation, and it is stated here so nobody plans around a guarantee that
cannot exist.

### How fresh it is

Tags are read **on each run** of a suite against that table and cached on the
asset. So a newly-classified column takes effect from the suite's next run —
including on samples captured *before* it was tagged, because a classification is
a statement about the data rather than about the moment it was read.

If the tags cannot be read — no permission on the tag, a warehouse that is down —
DataQ logs it and behaves exactly as it did before the tag existed. It never
infers a clearance from a failed lookup, because a wrong guess in that direction
un-masks data.

### Fail-closed mode

For a dataset where "unclassified" should mean "do not show", set
`require_classification` on the suite's column policy. Nothing row-level is then
surfaced unless a column is explicitly cleared — by a `public`-family tag or by
your own `identifier_column`. The classifier is not consulted at all, which is the
point: a column called `field_7` full of national ID numbers looks harmless to a
name heuristic.

It is off by default, and deliberately: a fully-masked failing row is
unactionable, so this is a trade you make for a regulated dataset rather than one
made for you.

## Data residency"""

The governance-tag floor has been threaded through every redaction call site since #415 and populated by **nothing**. This populates it: DataQ reads the classification a customer has already applied *in their warehouse* and treats it as the rung a suite policy cannot lift — on **REST and MCP** alike.

## A fixed convention, not a per-connection mapping

Per the decision on this issue. A mapping would be more flexible and worse: every deployment would express the same idea differently, the mapping would itself become an **unreviewed security control**, and one typo in it would silently un-mask a column.

`dataq_classification` on the column, using the vocabulary the redactor already speaks — plus Snowflake's own **`PRIVACY_CATEGORY`**, which costs nothing extra (same query) and is assigned by the warehouse itself.

**An unrecognised value is ignored, not guessed at.** Guessing has two directions and one of them un-masks data. `internal` is the worked example: it *sounds* like a classification, is commonly the default stamp on everything, and as a clearance would clear whole tables in exactly the organisations careful enough to tag them.

## Three design decisions worth the review

**Cached on the ASSET, not on each result.** A classification is a statement about the *data*, not about the moment it was read — so a tag applied today must mask samples captured yesterday. Freezing the map onto each result would have made a governance action apply only to future runs, silently. There's a test for exactly this.

**Read at run time, never at read time.** The read path must not open a warehouse connection — latency, and results have to stay readable when the warehouse is down. The run is already connected with the credentials and resolved target in hand.

**Every failure is silence.** No permission on the tag, a missing `information_schema`, a dead warehouse → `{}` and a log line. Never an exception into a run, and never an inferred clearance. That direction matters more than usual: **fail-closed mode treats a non-sensitive tag as a clearance**, so a fetcher that guessed on failure could *un-mask* data. Silence degrades to exactly the pre-G3 behaviour.

## Scope limit, stated rather than left to be discovered

Only **Snowflake** and **Unity Catalog** have a column-tag concept. For ADLS, S3, Iceberg and flat files the classification remains the suite policy, the classifier and fail-closed mode. That's a platform limit, not an implementation gap — documented so nobody plans around a guarantee that cannot exist.

# ── Review findings (PR #1468) ────────────────────────────────────────────────


def test_a_failed_tag_read_does_not_erase_the_cached_map(db_session: Any, monkeypatch: Any) -> None:
    """The worst of the review findings, and it inverted the safety property the
    module's own docstring claimed.

    A failed fetch used to return `{}`, which the refresh wrote straight over the
    cached map — so a permission error on the tag would **un-mask columns that
    were masked a minute earlier**. "I could not look" and "I looked and there is
    nothing" have to be different answers, because only one of them is safe to
    write down.
    """
    from backend.app.services import column_tags as ct

    run = _seed(db_session, tags={"vendor_name": "sensitive"})
    suite = db_session.get(Suite, run.suite_id)
    asset = db_session.get(Asset, suite.asset_id)
    connection = db_session.get(Connection, suite.connection_id)
    # Past the TTL, so the refresh actually attempts a read.
    asset.column_tags_refreshed_at = datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(days=1)
    db_session.commit()

    monkeypatch.setattr(ct, "fetch_column_tags", lambda *a, **k: None)

    class _Target:
        table = "ORDERS"
        schema = "RETAIL"
        catalog = None

    ct.refresh_asset_column_tags(
        db_session,
        suite=suite,
        connection=connection,
        target=_Target(),
        secret_store=object(),  # type: ignore[arg-type]
    )

    db_session.expire_all()
    assert db_session.get(Asset, asset.id).column_tags == {"vendor_name": "sensitive"}


def test_a_successful_empty_read_does_clear_the_map(db_session: Any, monkeypatch: Any) -> None:
    """The other half — otherwise "never erase" becomes "never update".

    Un-tagging a column in the warehouse is a real governance action, and it has
    to take effect. This is the case that distinguishes a cautious cache from a
    write-once one.
    """
    from backend.app.services import column_tags as ct

    run = _seed(db_session, tags={"vendor_name": "sensitive"})
    suite = db_session.get(Suite, run.suite_id)
    asset = db_session.get(Asset, suite.asset_id)
    connection = db_session.get(Connection, suite.connection_id)
    asset.column_tags_refreshed_at = datetime.now(UTC) - timedelta(days=1)
    db_session.commit()

    monkeypatch.setattr(ct, "fetch_column_tags", lambda *a, **k: {})

    class _Target:
        table = "ORDERS"
        schema = "RETAIL"
        catalog = None

    ct.refresh_asset_column_tags(
        db_session,
        suite=suite,
        connection=connection,
        target=_Target(),
        secret_store=object(),  # type: ignore[arg-type]
    )

    db_session.expire_all()
    assert db_session.get(Asset, asset.id).column_tags == {}


def test_a_retargeted_suite_does_not_re_redact_old_runs_against_the_new_table(
    client: TestClient, db_session: Any
) -> None:
    """Tags are anchored on the RUN's asset, not the suite's current one.

    A suite can be retargeted at a different table; the runs it already produced
    are samples of the OLD one. Redacting them against the new table's
    classifications applies the wrong governance to the wrong data — and in the
    direction this test exercises, it would expose values that the table they
    actually came from had classified.
    """
    run = _seed(db_session, tags={"vendor_name": "sensitive"})
    suite = db_session.get(Suite, run.suite_id)
    run_row = db_session.get(Run, run.id)
    run_row.asset_id = suite.asset_id  # what this run actually read

    # The suite is now pointed at a different table, whose columns are untagged.
    other = Asset(
        namespace=f"snowflake://acct-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:6]}",
        name="RETAIL.INVOICES",
        env="dev",
        column_tags={},
    )
    db_session.add(other)
    db_session.flush()
    suite.asset_id = other.id
    db_session.commit()

    body = _sample(client, run)
    assert "ACME LTD" not in str(body["sample_failures"]), (
        "the old run's sample must stay masked by the classification of the table "
        "it was actually read from"
    )


def test_alert_delivery_honours_the_tag_floor(db_session: Any) -> None:
    """The sibling door that leaves the platform.

    An alert goes to a webhook or a mailbox whose location DataQ does not know, so
    a governance floor honoured in the UI and not in the outbound message is
    honoured in the place that matters least.
    """
    from backend.app.alerting.builder import build_run_report

    run = _seed(db_session, tags={"vendor_name": "sensitive"})
    run_row = db_session.get(Run, run.id)
    suite = db_session.get(Suite, run.suite_id)
    run_row.asset_id = suite.asset_id
    db_session.commit()

    report = build_run_report(db_session, run_row)
    assert "ACME LTD" not in str([r.sample_summary for r in report.results])

fixup: all eight /code-review findings on the warehouse tag reader (#433)

The first one inverted the safety property the module's own docstring claimed.

1. **A failed read erased the cache.** `fetch_column_tags` returned `{}` for
   "could not read", and the refresh wrote that straight over the cached map — so
   a permission error on the tag would UN-MASK columns that were masked a minute
   earlier, on a path whose docstring said it degrades gracefully. It now returns
   `None` for "could not look", distinct from `{}` for "looked, found nothing",
   and only the latter is written down. Both directions are tested: a failed read
   keeps the map, a successful empty read clears it — otherwise "never erase"
   quietly becomes "never update", and un-tagging a column in the warehouse would
   stop working.

2. **Alerts did not get the tag floor.** Applied on REST and MCP and not on the
   surface that LEAVES the platform, into a webhook or mailbox whose location
   DataQ does not know — honoured everywhere except where it matters most.

3. Same for MCP `dryrun_check`: the tag would mask the column in the record and
   expose it in the rehearsal.

4. **Tags were anchored on `suite.asset_id`, not `run.asset_id`.** A retargeted
   suite's older runs are samples of the PREVIOUS table, so they were being
   redacted against the new table's classifications — the wrong governance
   applied to the wrong data, in both directions.

5. **No `LEVEL = 'COLUMN'` filter on the Snowflake query.** Snowflake tags are
   inherited, so one `dataq_classification = 'public'` on a schema arrived as a
   per-column clearance for every column beneath it — and in fail-closed mode a
   clearance is exactly what un-masks.

6. Identifier case: Snowflake folds unquoted names upper, Unity Catalog lower.
   A mismatched target resolved to nothing and returned silently empty, which is
   indistinguishable from "no tags".

7. The tag name is matched without its namespace — documented as a limit of the
   convention rather than left implicit.

8. An unconditional warehouse connect per run, with `column_tags_refreshed_at`
   written and never read. Now a 15-minute TTL: the timestamp does the job it was
   added for, and a frequently-scheduled suite stops re-reading a map that
   changes when a human edits governance.

Four mutations, each killing its own test — including the cache-erase and the
alerting door.

**And one defect of my own, found by the full suite rather than the review:** the
new module's `_seed` sets a `get_current_user` override, and three of its tests
take `db_session` without the `client` fixture that cleared it. The override
leaked into later modules, where a test authenticated as a `User` whose row had
been rolled back and hit a `ForeignKeyViolation`. Fixed with an autouse teardown
— a helper that mutates global state has to be paired with cleanup that runs
regardless of what the test remembered to request.

Full suite 4797 passed. Black / Ruff / mypy / Bandit clean.

Refs #433, #1468.

G3's warehouse half is built — [PR #1468](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1468), CI running.

## What shipped

Both platforms, per your decision. **Snowflake** reads `dataq_classification` plus Snowflake's own `PRIVACY_CATEGORY`; **Unity Catalog** reads `dataq_classification`. Tags cache on the asset at run time and feed the governance floor on **REST, MCP and alert delivery**.

**Documented convention, not configurable** — as you chose. The reasoning is now in `docs/security.md` for customers: a mapping would make itself an unreviewed security control where one typo un-masks a column.

## The review found 8 things, and one inverted my own safety claim

**A failed tag read *erased* the cache.** I returned `{}` for "couldn't read", and the refresh wrote that over the cached map — so a permission error would **un-mask columns that were masked a minute earlier**, on a path whose docstring said it degraded gracefully. Now `None` means "couldn't look" and only `{}` gets written down. Both directions are tested, because the obvious fix breaks the other one: without a second test, "never erase" silently becomes "never update".

Two more were doors I'd guarded on one side only — **alerts** (the surface that actually leaves the platform) and MCP's **dry-run**. And `LEVEL = 'COLUMN'` was missing on the Snowflake query, so an inherited schema-level `public` tag would have cleared every column beneath it.

I also introduced a test-pollution bug the review didn't catch — my `_seed` set a global auth override that leaked into later modules. The full suite caught it; an autouse teardown fixes it.

## What's honestly not done

**Nothing has run against a real warehouse.** Two things only a live run settles:

1. whether the connection's role can read `TAG_REFERENCES_ALL_COLUMNS` (vs needing `ACCOUNT_USAGE`, which lags up to 2h);
2. whether `system`-catalog access is granted for UC's `column_tags`.

Given how many of this session's bugs were invisible outside a real environment, I'd treat the SQL as unproven. **#433 should stay open until verification.** The compliance register says so rather than implying a green suite is evidence.

**When you want to verify:** waking the harness is ~CAD 17/day for Azure, Snowflake separate. Tell me when it's up and I'll tag a real column on both platforms and confirm end-to-end.
Both warehouses have local mirror connections. Let me verify the **real code path** read-only — this mutates nothing and settles the biggest unknown.

"""Read-only live check of G3's tag reader against the real warehouses.

Exercises `column_tags.fetch_column_tags` — the actual shipped code path, not a
hand-written query — against the Snowflake and Unity Catalog connections in the
local mirror. Purely a SELECT (a table function / information_schema read); it
creates nothing and changes nothing.

What it settles:
  * does the statement even execute (syntax, dialect)?
  * does the connection's role have permission to read tags?
  * what comes back on a table with no tags — clean empty, or an error?
"""

import sys

sys.path.insert(0, ".")

from sqlalchemy import select  # noqa: E402

from backend.app.core.secrets import get_secret_store  # noqa: E402
from backend.app.db.models import Connection, Suite  # noqa: E402
from backend.app.db.session import SessionLocal  # noqa: E402
from backend.app.services import column_tags, run_target  # noqa: E402

session = SessionLocal()
store = get_secret_store()

for conn_type in ("snowflake", "unity_catalog"):
    conn = session.scalar(select(Connection).where(Connection.type == conn_type))
    if conn is None:
        print(f"\n[{conn_type}] no connection configured — skipped")
        continue

    suite = session.scalar(select(Suite).where(Suite.connection_id == conn.id))
    if suite is None or not suite.target:
        print(f"\n[{conn_type}] no suite with a target — skipped")
        continue

    try:
        target = run_target.resolve_target(conn.type, suite.target)
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"\n[{conn_type}] target unresolvable: {type(exc).__name__}")
        continue

    print(f"\n[{conn_type}] connection={conn.name!r} table={getattr(target, 'table', None)!r}")
    result = column_tags.fetch_column_tags(
        conn,
        table=str(getattr(target, "table", "")),
        schema=getattr(target, "schema", None),
        catalog=getattr(target, "catalog", None),
        secret_store=store,
    )
    if result is None:
        print(f"  -> None  (COULD NOT READ — see the column_tags_unavailable log line)")
    else:
        print(f"  -> {len(result)} tagged column(s): {result}")
        print("     (query executed and permission granted)")

session.close()

"""LIVE verification of G3's warehouse tag reader — #433.

Runs the SHIPPED code path (`column_tags.fetch_column_tags`) against real
Snowflake and Unity Catalog, in the production shape:

  * governance is applied by a privileged role (the loader), as an organisation's
    data steward would;
  * the tag is read back through DataQ's own reader connection, which is what the
    product actually uses.

That split is the point. A test that both writes and reads as the same powerful
role would prove nothing about whether DataQ's least-privileged connection can
see a tag someone else applied — which is the whole question.

Credentials arrive via env vars populated inline from Key Vault at call time and
are never written anywhere. Every statement is cleaned up in a `finally`.

Usage (all env supplied by the caller):
  SF_SECRET=... UC_SECRET=... SF_ADMIN_SECRET=... python verify.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import os
import sys
import uuid

sys.path.insert(0, ".")

from sqlalchemy import select, text  # noqa: E402

from backend.app.db.models import Connection  # noqa: E402
from backend.app.db.session import SessionLocal  # noqa: E402
from backend.app.services import column_tags  # noqa: E402

TAG_NAME = "dataq_classification"


class _StaticStore:
    """A SecretStore returning one value, for one ref, in this process only."""

    def __init__(self, value: str) -> None:
        self._value = value

    def get(self, name: str) -> str:
        return self._value

    def set(self, name: str, value: str) -> None:  # pragma: no cover
        raise RuntimeError("verification never writes a secret")

    def delete(self, name: str) -> None:  # pragma: no cover
        raise RuntimeError("verification never deletes a secret")


def _open(conn: Connection, secret: str):
    from backend.app.services.profile_service import _open_connection

    return _open_connection(conn, _StaticStore(secret))


def verify_snowflake(session, sf_secret: str, admin_secret: str | None) -> None:
    conn = session.scalar(select(Connection).where(Connection.type == "snowflake"))
    if conn is None:
        print("[snowflake] no connection — skipped")
        return
    cfg = conn.config or {}
    db, schema = cfg.get("database"), cfg.get("schema")
    table = os.environ.get("SF_TABLE", "ORDERS_HEADER")
    column = os.environ.get("SF_COLUMN", "CUSTOMER_ID")
    tag = f"{TAG_NAME}"

    print(f"\n=== SNOWFLAKE {db}.{schema}.{table} ===")

    # 1. Read-only first: does the statement execute at all, and does DataQ's
    #    own reader role have permission? This is the unknown that matters most,
    #    and it is answered without changing anything.
    before = column_tags.fetch_column_tags(
        conn, table=table, schema=schema, secret_store=_StaticStore(sf_secret)
    )
    print(f"[read as DataQ's role] -> {before!r}")
    if before is None:
        print("  RESULT: could NOT read tags (permission or syntax). See the log line above.")
    else:
        print(f"  RESULT: query executed; {len(before)} tagged column(s) visible")

    if not admin_secret:
        print("  (no admin credential supplied — skipping the apply/read-back half)")
        return

    # 2. Apply a tag as the privileged role, read it back as DataQ's role.
    applied = False
    try:
        with _open(conn, admin_secret) as admin:
            admin.execute(text(f"CREATE TAG IF NOT EXISTS {db}.{schema}.{tag}"))
            admin.execute(
                text(f"ALTER TABLE {db}.{schema}.{table} MODIFY COLUMN {column} "
                     f"SET TAG {db}.{schema}.{tag} = 'pii'")
            )
            applied = True
        print(f"[applied] {tag}='pii' on {column} (as the privileged role)")

        after = column_tags.fetch_column_tags(
            conn, table=table, schema=schema, secret_store=_StaticStore(sf_secret)
        )
        print(f"[read back as DataQ's role] -> {after!r}")
        expected = column.lower()
        if after and after.get(expected) == column_tags.SENSITIVE:
            print(f"  ✅ VERIFIED: {expected} reads as SENSITIVE through the shipped code path")
        else:
            print(f"  ❌ NOT VERIFIED: expected {expected!r} -> 'sensitive', got {after!r}")
    finally:
        if applied:
            try:
                with _open(conn, admin_secret) as admin:
                    admin.execute(
                        text(f"ALTER TABLE {db}.{schema}.{table} MODIFY COLUMN {column} "
                             f"UNSET TAG {db}.{schema}.{tag}")
                    )
                    admin.execute(text(f"DROP TAG IF EXISTS {db}.{schema}.{tag}"))
                print("[cleanup] tag unset and dropped")
            except Exception as exc:
                print(f"[cleanup] FAILED — manual cleanup needed: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")


def verify_unity_catalog(session, uc_secret: str) -> None:
    conn = session.scalar(select(Connection).where(Connection.type == "unity_catalog"))
    if conn is None:
        print("\n[unity_catalog] no connection — skipped")
        return
    catalog = os.environ.get("UC_CATALOG", "dataq_retail")
    schema = os.environ.get("UC_SCHEMA", "gold")
    table = os.environ.get("UC_TABLE", "feedback_sentiment")
    column = os.environ.get("UC_COLUMN", "customer_id")

    print(f"\n=== UNITY CATALOG {catalog}.{schema}.{table} ===")

    before = column_tags.fetch_column_tags(
        conn, table=table, schema=schema, catalog=catalog, secret_store=_StaticStore(uc_secret)
    )
    print(f"[read as DataQ's role] -> {before!r}")
    if before is None:
        print("  RESULT: could NOT read tags (permission on system tables, or syntax).")
    else:
        print(f"  RESULT: query executed; {len(before)} tagged column(s) visible")

    applied = False
    try:
        with _open(conn, uc_secret) as c:
            c.execute(
                text(f"ALTER TABLE {catalog}.{schema}.{table} ALTER COLUMN {column} "
                     f"SET TAGS ('{TAG_NAME}' = 'pii')")
            )
            applied = True
        print(f"[applied] {TAG_NAME}='pii' on {column}")

        after = column_tags.fetch_column_tags(
            conn, table=table, schema=schema, catalog=catalog, secret_store=_StaticStore(uc_secret)
        )
        print(f"[read back] -> {after!r}")
        if after and after.get(column.lower()) == column_tags.SENSITIVE:
            print(f"  ✅ VERIFIED: {column.lower()} reads as SENSITIVE through the shipped path")
        else:
            print(f"  ❌ NOT VERIFIED: expected {column.lower()!r} -> 'sensitive', got {after!r}")
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"[apply] failed: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")
    finally:
        if applied:
            try:
                with _open(conn, uc_secret) as c:
                    c.execute(
                        text(f"ALTER TABLE {catalog}.{schema}.{table} ALTER COLUMN {column} "
                             f"UNSET TAGS ('{TAG_NAME}')")
                    )
                print("[cleanup] tag unset")
            except Exception as exc:
                print(f"[cleanup] FAILED — manual cleanup needed: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")


def main() -> None:
    session = SessionLocal()
    try:
        sf = os.environ.get("SF_SECRET")
        uc = os.environ.get("UC_SECRET")
        admin = os.environ.get("SF_ADMIN_SECRET")
        if sf:
            verify_snowflake(session, sf, admin)
        else:
            print("[snowflake] SF_SECRET not supplied — skipped")
        if uc:
            verify_unity_catalog(session, uc)
        else:
            print("[unity_catalog] UC_SECRET not supplied — skipped")
    finally:
        session.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Warehouse-native column classification — G3 / #433, the authoritative source.

`run_service`'s redaction ladder has always had a **governance-tag floor** as its
top rung (`_tag_sensitive` / `_tag_non_sensitive`), threaded through every call
site and populated by nothing. This module is what populates it: it reads the
classification a customer has already applied **in their warehouse**, so
DataQ's masking follows the organisation's own data governance instead of a name
heuristic guessing at it.

## The convention (fixed, not configurable)

DataQ honours a **documented convention** rather than a per-connection mapping.
A mapping would be more flexible and worse: every deployment would express the
same idea differently, the mapping itself would become an unreviewed security
control, and a typo in it would silently un-mask a column. One convention is
checkable by reading this file.

**Tag key** — `dataq_classification` on the COLUMN, matched case-insensitively.

**Tag values** — the same vocabulary the redactor already speaks:

* masks: ``sensitive`` · ``pii`` · ``confidential`` · ``restricted`` · ``secret``
* clears: ``public`` · ``non_sensitive`` · ``nonsensitive``

Anything else is **ignored rather than guessed at** — an unrecognised value means
the column falls through to the next rung of the ladder (suite policy, then the
classifier), which is where it would have been with no tag at all. Treating an
unknown value as a clearance is the one interpretation that could un-mask data,
so it is the one explicitly not taken.

**Snowflake additionally honours its own `PRIVACY_CATEGORY` system tag**, set by
Snowflake's built-in classification. It costs nothing extra — the same query
returns it — and it is the most authoritative signal available on that platform,
since the warehouse assigned it. Its values (`IDENTIFIER`, `QUASI_IDENTIFIER`,
`SENSITIVE`) all mean "personal data", so all three mask.

## What has no tag source at all

Only `snowflake` and `unity_catalog` have a column-tag concept. ADLS, S3, Iceberg
and flat files have none — there is no authoritative source to read — so for those

    Returns **`None` when the tags could not be read at all**: no permission on

    lacked it: the caller CACHES this result, so returning `{}` on failure would
    overwrite a previously-read map and **un-mask columns that were masked a
    minute ago**. "I could not look" and "I looked and there is nothing" have to
    be different answers, because only one of them is safe to write down.

    **Never raises.** A fetcher that failed loudly would take out a run over a
    governance lookup, and one that guessed could un-mask data through fail-closed
    mode's clearance path.

cat > /tmp/g3verify/verify_sf_final.py <<'PYEOF'
"""Snowflake half of G3's live verification — #433, with the CREATE TAG grant now in place.

Two identities, deliberately, because that split IS the test:

  * **DATAQ_LOADER** applies the tags — the steward role an organisation governs
    with, and the one just granted CREATE TAG.
  * **DataQ's own connection (DATAQ_READER)** reads them back through the shipped
    `column_tags.fetch_column_tags`, unchanged, resolving its credential through
    the real SecretStore.

If one role did both, the run would prove nothing about whether the
least-privileged connection the product actually runs as can see a tag someone
else applied — which is the entire question.

Four properties are under test, and only a live warehouse can settle any of them:
  1. a column tag round-trips through the shipped query at all;
  2. Snowflake's UPPER-cased column names fold to the lower-cased keys the
     redactor matches on;
  3. `LEVEL = 'COLUMN'` actually suppresses an INHERITED table-level tag — the
     review finding, and the one that could UN-MASK data if wrong;
  4. an unrecognised tag value is ignored rather than guessed at.

Everything created is removed in a `finally`, and removal is then VERIFIED by
re-reading rather than assumed from the absence of an exception.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import os
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, ".")

import snowflake.connector as sc
from backend.app.core.secrets import get_secret_store
from backend.app.db.models import Connection
from backend.app.db.session import SessionLocal
from backend.app.services import column_tags
from sqlalchemy import select

TAG = column_tags.DATAQ_TAG_KEY
TABLE = "ORDERS_HEADER"
PII_COLUMN = "CUSTOMER_ID"
JUNK_COLUMN = "ORDER_ID"          # gets an unrecognised value; must stay absent
STEWARD_ROLE = "DATAQ_LOADER"


def main() -> int:
    session = SessionLocal()
    store = get_secret_store()
    conn = session.scalar(
        select(Connection).where(Connection.type == "snowflake", Connection.name == "Retail Snowflake DEV")
    )
    assert conn is not None, "Retail Snowflake DEV connection missing from the mirror"
    cfg = dict(conn.config or {})
    db, schema, wh, acct, user = (
        cfg["database"], cfg["schema"], cfg.get("warehouse"), cfg["account"], cfg["user"],
    )
    fq_tag = f"{db}.{schema}.{TAG}"
    print(f"=== SNOWFLAKE {db}.{schema}.{TABLE} ===")
    print(f"    steward = {STEWARD_ROLE}   reader = {cfg.get('role')} (DataQ's own connection)")

    steward = sc.connect(
        account=acct, user=user, password=os.environ["SF_STEWARD_SECRET"],
        role=STEWARD_ROLE, warehouse=wh, database=db, schema=schema, login_timeout=30,
    )
    cur = steward.cursor()
    print(f"[steward] connected as role {cur.execute('select current_role()').fetchone()[0]}")

    created = applied_col = applied_tbl = applied_junk = False
    failures: list[str] = []
    try:
        cur.execute(f"CREATE TAG IF NOT EXISTS {fq_tag}")
        created = True
        print(f"[steward] tag {fq_tag} created")

        cur.execute(
            f"ALTER TABLE {db}.{schema}.{TABLE} MODIFY COLUMN {PII_COLUMN} SET TAG {fq_tag} = 'pii'"
        )
        applied_col = True
        print(f"[steward] {TAG}='pii' on COLUMN {PII_COLUMN}")

        # Property 3: an inherited table-level tag carrying a CLEARANCE value.
        # Snowflake reports table tags against every column beneath them, so
        # without LEVEL='COLUMN' this would arrive as a per-column 'public' —
        # and in fail-closed mode a clearance is exactly what un-masks data.
        cur.execute(f"ALTER TABLE {db}.{schema}.{TABLE} SET TAG {fq_tag} = 'public'")
        applied_tbl = True
        print(f"[steward] {TAG}='public' on the TABLE (inherited — must be suppressed)")

        # Property 4: a value outside the vocabulary must fall through, not clear.
        cur.execute(
            f"ALTER TABLE {db}.{schema}.{TABLE} MODIFY COLUMN {JUNK_COLUMN} SET TAG {fq_tag} = 'banana'"
        )
        applied_junk = True
        print(f"[steward] {TAG}='banana' on COLUMN {JUNK_COLUMN} (unrecognised — must be ignored)")

        got = column_tags.fetch_column_tags(
            conn, table=TABLE, schema=schema, secret_store=store
        )
        print(f"\n[read back as {cfg.get('role')} through the shipped path] -> {got!r}\n")

        if got is None:
            failures.append("fetch returned None — the reader could not read tags at all")
        else:
            if got.get(PII_COLUMN.lower()) == column_tags.SENSITIVE:
                print(f"  ✅ 1+2  {PII_COLUMN.lower()!r} -> 'sensitive'  (round-trip + UPPER->lower folding)")
            else:
                failures.append(f"expected {PII_COLUMN.lower()!r} -> 'sensitive', got {got.get(PII_COLUMN.lower())!r}")

            if column_tags.NON_SENSITIVE not in got.values():
                print("  ✅ 3    the inherited table-level 'public' produced NO column clearance (LEVEL filter holds)")
            else:
                failures.append(f"LEVEL='COLUMN' filter FAILED — inherited clearance leaked: {got!r}")

            if JUNK_COLUMN.lower() not in got:
                print(f"  ✅ 4    unrecognised 'banana' ignored — {JUNK_COLUMN.lower()!r} absent, falls through the ladder")
            else:
                failures.append(f"unrecognised value was interpreted: {JUNK_COLUMN.lower()} -> {got[JUNK_COLUMN.lower()]!r}")
    finally:
        for label, sql in (
            ("table tag", f"ALTER TABLE {db}.{schema}.{TABLE} UNSET TAG {fq_tag}" if applied_tbl else None),
            ("pii column tag", f"ALTER TABLE {db}.{schema}.{TABLE} MODIFY COLUMN {PII_COLUMN} UNSET TAG {fq_tag}" if applied_col else None),
            ("junk column tag", f"ALTER TABLE {db}.{schema}.{TABLE} MODIFY COLUMN {JUNK_COLUMN} UNSET TAG {fq_tag}" if applied_junk else None),
            ("tag object", f"DROP TAG IF EXISTS {fq_tag}" if created else None),
        ):
            if sql is None:
                continue
            try:
                cur.execute(sql)
            except Exception as exc:
                print(f"[cleanup] ⚠️ {label} FAILED — manual cleanup needed: {exc}")

        # Cleanup is verified, not assumed.
        after = column_tags.fetch_column_tags(conn, table=TABLE, schema=schema, secret_store=store)
        print(f"\n[cleanup verified by re-reading] -> {after!r}  {'✅ clean' if after == {} else '⚠️ residue'}")
        cur.close(); steward.close(); session.close()

    if failures:
        print("\n❌ NOT VERIFIED:")
        for f in failures:
            print(f"   - {f}")
        return 1
    print("\n✅ SNOWFLAKE VERIFIED — all four properties hold against the live warehouse")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

are very different worlds and only one of them makes the filter necessary.

protecting against nothing and property 3 was vacuous.

from __future__ import annotations
import os, sys
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import snowflake.connector as sc

DB, SCHEMA, TABLE, TAG = "DATAQ_DB", "RETAIL", "PAYMENTS", "dataq_classification"
FQ = f"{DB}.{SCHEMA}.{TAG}"
BASE = ("SELECT COLUMN_NAME, TAG_NAME, TAG_VALUE, LEVEL "
        f"FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TAG_REFERENCES_ALL_COLUMNS('{DB}.{SCHEMA}.{TABLE}', 'TABLE'))")

                     warehouse="DATAQ_WH", database=DB, schema=SCHEMA, login_timeout=30)

                    password=os.environ["SF_READER_SECRET"], role="DATAQ_READER",
                    warehouse="DATAQ_WH", database=DB, schema=SCHEMA, login_timeout=30)
sc_cur, rd_cur = steward.cursor(), reader.cursor()
applied = False
try:
    sc_cur.execute(f"CREATE TAG IF NOT EXISTS {FQ}")
    sc_cur.execute(f"ALTER TABLE {DB}.{SCHEMA}.{TABLE} SET TAG {FQ} = 'public'")
    applied = True
    print(f"[steward] TABLE-level {TAG}='public' applied (no column tags at all)\n")

    unfiltered = rd_cur.execute(BASE).fetchall()
    filtered = rd_cur.execute(BASE + " WHERE LEVEL = 'COLUMN'").fetchall()

    print(f"WITHOUT the filter -> {len(unfiltered)} row(s)")
    for r in unfiltered[:5]:
        print(f"   column={r[0]:16} tag={r[1]:22} value={r[2]!r:12} LEVEL={r[3]!r}")
    if len(unfiltered) > 5:
        print(f"   ... and {len(unfiltered) - 5} more, all inherited from the table")
    print(f"\nWITH the shipped filter -> {len(filtered)} row(s)")

    leaked = [r for r in unfiltered if str(r[2]).lower() == "public"]
    if leaked and not filtered:
        print(f"\n✅ FILTER IS LOAD-BEARING — {len(leaked)} inherited clearance row(s) would have")
        print("   reached the redactor as per-column 'public' and UN-MASKED those columns.")
        print("   Property 3 was a real test, not a vacuous pass.")
    elif not leaked:
        print("\n⚠️ INCONCLUSIVE — the warehouse reported no inherited rows even unfiltered,")
        print("   so property 3 proved nothing about the filter.")
    else:
        print("\n❌ the filter did NOT suppress the inherited rows")
finally:
    if applied:
        try:
            sc_cur.execute(f"ALTER TABLE {DB}.{SCHEMA}.{TABLE} UNSET TAG {FQ}")
            sc_cur.execute(f"DROP TAG IF EXISTS {FQ}")
            print("\n[cleanup] table tag unset, tag dropped")
        except Exception as exc:

    left = sc_cur.execute(f"SHOW TAGS IN SCHEMA {DB}.{SCHEMA}").fetchall()
    print(f"[cleanup verified] tags remaining in {DB}.{SCHEMA}: {len(left)}")
    sc_cur.close(); rd_cur.close(); steward.close(); reader.close()

p = "docs/compliance-posture.md"
s = open(p).read()

s = s.replace(
    "### G3 — 🟢 Authoritative PII/PHI classification (not just a heuristic) — #433 — **warehouse tags consumed; verification pending**",
    "### G3 — 🟢 Authoritative PII/PHI classification (not just a heuristic) — #433 — **warehouse tags consumed, live-verified on both platforms**",
)

old_start = "**Live-verified 2026-08-18 against the real warehouses**"
i = s.index(old_start)
j = s.index("### G4 —")
new = """**Live-verified 2026-08-18 against the real warehouses**, which is the only evidence that
counts across a driver boundary (the #953 rule). Every property is now settled on **both**
platforms, each in the production shape — a **steward** role applies the tag, and DataQ's
own least-privileged connection reads it back through the shipped `fetch_column_tags`. That
split is the test: one powerful role doing both would prove nothing about whether the role
the product actually runs as can see a tag someone else applied.

* **Unity Catalog — verified end to end.** `dataq_classification = 'pii'` applied to a real
  column, read back as `{'customer_id': 'sensitive'}`, then removed — with the removal
  confirmed by re-reading `information_schema.column_tags`, not by trusting the cleanup's
  own log line.
* **Snowflake — verified end to end**, on a `DATAQ_LOADER`-owned table, once that role was
  granted `CREATE TAG`. Four properties, none of which a unit test can reach:
  1. a column tag round-trips through the shipped query at all;
  2. Snowflake's `UPPER`-cased column names fold to the lower-cased keys the redactor
     matches on (`PAYMENT_ID` → `payment_id` → `sensitive`);
  3. `LEVEL = 'COLUMN'` suppresses an **inherited** table-level tag;
  4. an unrecognised value (`'banana'`) is ignored rather than guessed at — the column is
     absent from the map and falls through to the next rung of the ladder.
* **`INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TAG_REFERENCES_ALL_COLUMNS` executes under `DATAQ_READER`**, so no
  `ACCOUNT_USAGE` grant is required and classifications are read **fresh**, without that
  view's up-to-two-hour lag.

**Property 3 was then mutation-checked, because it could have passed vacuously.** "The
inherited tag produced no clearance" is equally true if the warehouse simply never reports
inherited tags — in which case the filter guards nothing. Running the same query with the
filter removed settled it: one table-level `dataq_classification = 'public'` came back as
**six rows, one per column, each `LEVEL = 'TABLE'`**, and the shipped query returned zero.
Without the filter those six would have reached the redactor as per-column clearances and
**un-masked every column in the table** — under fail-closed mode, where a clearance is
precisely what lifts the mask. The guard is load-bearing, and the test is real.

**Two findings the live run produced that no amount of local reasoning would have.**
Applying a tag needs **`OWNERSHIP` of the table**, not merely `CREATE TAG` on the schema —
the first attempt was refused on an `ACCOUNTADMIN`-owned table and succeeded on a
loader-owned one. And a **role-scoped programmatic access token cannot assume another
role**, even one the underlying user is granted; this is why the earlier pass could not
apply anything at all. Both are properties of the platform's privilege model, and both are
now on the record rather than rediscovered by the next person.

**Still unexercised, deliberately:** Snowflake's own `PRIVACY_CATEGORY` system tag. It is
set by Snowflake's built-in classification service, not by an `ALTER TABLE`, so exercising
it means running that service — and the code path it feeds is the same `_merge` the
`dataq_classification` cases just proved. Recorded as a limit rather than claimed as tested.

result.output:
if a column is classified in the warehouse, DataQ reads that classification and
treats it as the floor — a suite-level setting cannot lift it.

### The convention

A **fixed, documented convention**, not a per-connection mapping. A mapping would
be more flexible and worse: every deployment would express the same idea
differently, the mapping itself would become an unreviewed security control, and a
typo in it would silently un-mask a column.

Tag your **columns** with the key **`dataq_classification`** (matched
case-insensitively):

| Value | Effect |
|---|---|
| `sensitive` · `pii` · `confidential` · `restricted` · `secret` | **Always masked.** A suite policy cannot show it |
| `public` · `non_sensitive` · `nonsensitive` | Cleared — may be shown, unless the value itself is affirmatively personal data |
| anything else | **Ignored**, exactly as if untagged — see below |

**Snowflake additionally honours its own `PRIVACY_CATEGORY`**, set by Snowflake's
built-in classification. Its values (`IDENTIFIER`, `QUASI_IDENTIFIER`,
`SENSITIVE`) all mean personal data, so all three mask. It has no clearing side:
Snowflake omits the tag for data it does not consider personal rather than marking
it public, so an unexpected value means *unknown*, not *safe*.

**An unrecognised value is ignored rather than guessed at.** Guessing has only two
directions, and one of them un-masks data. `internal` is the worked example: it
sounds like a classification and is commonly the default stamp on everything, so
reading it as a clearance would clear whole tables in exactly the organisations
careful enough to tag them.

**Inherited tags are not read.** A tag applied to a table or schema is reported by
the warehouse against every column beneath it; DataQ accepts only tags applied to
the **column itself**. An inherited tag is a statement about the container, and
reading one as a per-column clearance would clear a whole schema from a single
misplaced `public`.

**The tag name is matched without its namespace**, and that is a constraint on
you rather than a feature: DataQ honours a tag *named* `dataq_classification`
wherever it lives, because knowing which database or schema should be
authoritative would require per-deployment configuration, and this convention is
deliberately fixed. **Do not create tags with this name for any other purpose** —
a same-named tag elsewhere carrying a `public`-family value would be honoured as
a clearance.

Only **Snowflake** and **Unity Catalog** have a column-tag concept. ADLS, S3,
Iceberg and flat files have no authoritative source to read, so for those the
classification remains the suite's own policy, the name/value classifier, and
fail-closed mode. This is a limit of the platforms, not a gap in the
implementation, and it is stated here so nobody plans around a guarantee that
cannot exist.

### How fresh it is

Tags are read **on each run** of a suite against that table and cached on the
asset. So a newly-classified column takes effect from the suite's next run —

Both stored Snowflake credentials are **role-scoped programmatic access tokens** — one `DATAQ_READER`, one `DATAQ_LOADER`. What remains unproven is narrow and specific: the **`LEVEL = 'COLUMN'` filter** and the **upper→lower column-name folding**, against real Snowflake rows. Closing it needs either a `CREATE TAG` grant on the target schema or an admin credential — a deliberate privilege decision, so I did not make it.

The failure is itself a small piece of evidence for the design: least-privileged roles genuinely cannot apply governance, which is exactly the separation this feature assumes.

The second roll carried two post-deploy-smoke findings from the first: **#1286** (the fix’s own regression — a 150px bound wrapped the copy button and grew every pipeline-runs row 56px→77px; measured the threshold on live prod and shipped 120) and **#1285** (pre-existing — orchestration poll failures were classified through the datasource message set, so both Airflow connections said “missing warehouse or role … check the suite’s run target” while the harness Airflow app was simply Stopped; an orchestration connection has none of those four things). The Snowflake half is closed. Summary while CI finishes:

## The grant unblocked it — and the loop is closed

`DATAQ_LOADER` + `CREATE TAG` was necessary but **not sufficient**: the first run still failed. Setting a tag on a column needs **`OWNERSHIP` of the table**, and `ORDERS_HEADER` is `ACCOUNTADMIN`-owned. The loader owns ten of the twelve `RETAIL` tables, so I moved to `PAYMENTS` rather than ask you for another grant — using a table the role already owns is the smaller change.

Four properties verified, steward applying and **DataQ's own `DATAQ_READER` connection** reading back through the shipped code:

1. the tag round-trips at all
2. `PAYMENT_ID` → `payment_id` → `sensitive` (`UPPER`→lower folding)
3. `LEVEL = 'COLUMN'` suppresses inherited tags
4. `'banana'` ignored, not guessed at

## Property 3 was mutation-checked, and it mattered

"No inherited clearance appeared" is equally true if the warehouse never reports inherited tags — in which case the filter guards nothing. Removing it:

```
WITHOUT the filter -> 6 row(s), all LEVEL='TABLE', all value='public'
WITH the shipped filter -> 0 row(s)
```

One misplaced table-level `public` would have reached the redactor as **six per-column clearances and un-masked every column** — under fail-closed mode, where a clearance is exactly what lifts the mask.

## Review caught me hedging, and the pushback was productive

I'd recorded `PRIVACY_CATEGORY` as "unexercised, same `_merge`". Wrong: it lives in the **shared `SNOWFLAKE` database**, a different access-control rule, and its failure is **silent** — zero rows, not an error, so the column reads as untagged and falls back to the name heuristic. Rather than caveat it, I tested it. The reviewer's conclusion (needs `IMPORTED PRIVILEGES`) is **disproven** — `DATAQ_READER` holds none and saw all three values correctly. The reasoning was still right, so that warning is now in the customer docs.

## Cleanliness — read back, not assumed

Tags in `DATAQ_DB.RETAIL`: **0** · tag references on `PAYMENTS`: **0** · `DATAQ_WH`: **SUSPENDED** · Databricks warehouse: **STOPPED** · 5 harness apps **Stopped**, both ADF triggers **Stopped**, all 7 jobs suspended with last executions still 2026-08-10/07-27. **The harness was never woken** — this needed only SaaS.

`CREATE TAG` is a permanent widening of the loader role, so it's recorded in [docs/ops-log.md](docs/ops-log.md) with both platform findings. #433 closes on merge. I'll confirm CI and merge when it lands.

## What the grant actually bought

`CREATE TAG` alone still failed — applying a tag needs **`OWNERSHIP` of the table**, and `ORDERS_HEADER` is `ACCOUNTADMIN`-owned. The loader owns ten of twelve `RETAIL` tables, so I used `PAYMENTS` instead of asking for a second grant.

Verified in the production shape (steward applies, DataQ's own `DATAQ_READER` reads back through the shipped code): round-trip · `PAYMENT_ID`→`payment_id` folding · `LEVEL='COLUMN'` suppressing inherited tags · unrecognised values ignored. Plus `PRIVACY_CATEGORY` on all three values.

**The mutation check is what makes property 3 mean anything.** Remove the filter and one table-level `public` returns **six rows, one per column** — each would have un-masked a column under fail-closed mode, where a clearance is precisely what lifts the mask.

I was wrong to write off `PRIVACY_CATEGORY` as "same `_merge`"; review caught it. It's a different access-control rule with a **silent** failure (zero rows, not an error). The reviewer's conclusion was also wrong — no `IMPORTED PRIVILEGES` needed, proven live — but the reasoning was right, so the warning is in the customer docs.

## Nothing left running or behind

Snowflake tags **0**, `DATAQ_WH` **SUSPENDED**, Databricks **STOPPED**, 5 harness apps **Stopped**, ADF triggers **Stopped**, 7 jobs suspended (last runs still 2026-08-10 / 07-27). **The harness was never woken** — this needed only SaaS, so no Azure state changed and nothing extra was billed. All confirmed by re-reading state, not by trusting cleanup logs.

The `CREATE TAG` grant is permanent, so it's in [docs/ops-log.md](docs/ops-log.md) alongside both platform findings — including that a **role-scoped PAT cannot assume another role**, which is what blocked yesterday's attempt and wears an authentication error's clothing while being an authorisation problem.

## Data residency

Where data lives, and what can take it elsewhere. GDPR Ch. V asks a controller to
answer both; this section is the answer for the reference deployments, and
`GET /api/v1/admin/deployment` is the same answer read live from a running
instance (workspace-admin only) so it can be checked rather than trusted.

**One declared jurisdiction per deployment.** The unit that matters is the
*jurisdiction* — the country whose law applies — because that is what GDPR Ch. V
keys on; a cloud *region* is how a provider spells a location within one. Both
reference deployments are entirely in the **United States**.

The primary region is set by a single IaC variable (`azure_location` /
`aws_region`) and declared to the app as `DEPLOYMENT_REGION`. The app's value is a
**declaration, not a verification** — software cannot confirm which datacentre its
database sits in — and it is reported as `null` when unset, so an auditor sees a
gap rather than a guess. Where an individual resource sits in a *different region
of the same jurisdiction*, the table below says so; those are recorded exceptions,
not drift.

### Where each resource sits

| Resource | Region | Holds customer data? |
|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL (AWS RDS) | the declared region | **Yes** — suites, checks, results, and the incidental personal data in failing-row samples |
| PostgreSQL (Azure Flexible Server) | **`West US 3`** — a recorded exception; the app's other resources are in `West US 2`. Same jurisdiction | **Yes** — as above |
| Secret store (Key Vault / Secrets Manager / OpenBao) | the declared region | Warehouse credentials, not customer data |
| Container Apps / ECS compute | the declared region | In transit only |
| Object storage (AWS landing bucket) | the declared region | Whatever the operator lands there |
| Telemetry (App Insights / CloudWatch / OTLP) | the sink's region — **operator-chosen** | Operational metadata; PII redacted at the logger |
| CloudFront (AWS only) | **global edge** | **No.** Only fingerprinted static assets are cached (`/assets/*.<ext>`); every other path is pass-through, so no API response and no failing-row sample is stored at an edge location |
| WAFv2 Web ACL (AWS only) | **`us-east-1`, unavoidably** | **No** — the ACL is rule configuration. CloudFront-scoped ACLs exist only in `us-east-1` regardless of where the stack lives |

The CloudFront and WAF rows are stated rather than omitted for the same reason: a
reviewer who finds a `us-east-1` provider alias in an `eu-west` stack should find
it explained here rather than have to work out whether it matters.

**The Azure Postgres row is a third recorded exception**, and the one that matters
most, because it is the resource holding the data.

The subscription caps PostgreSQL Flexible Servers at one, so the app shares the
harness's server and declares it as a `data` source — its region was fixed by
whoever created it, not by this stack. Verified against live Azure: **West US 3**,
while the app's own resources are in **West US 2**. Resolving it means a new
server plus a data migration against that same cap, so it is **accepted
deliberately** ([#1465](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1465))
rather than treated as a defect.

Accepted on a specific basis, which is the part worth checking: **same
jurisdiction**. Both regions are in the United States, so no personal data crosses
a border and GDPR Ch. V is not engaged. An operator whose regime cares about
sub-national placement — or who deploys into the EU, where a two-region split
could straddle adequacy boundaries — must treat this as a real constraint and
consolidate rather than inherit the exception.

The `check` block in `postgres.tf` compares the server against an explicitly
declared `shared_pg_expected_location` rather than against `azure_location`. That
distinction is what keeps it working: checking against `azure_location` would warn
on every plan forever, and a permanently-firing check is noise people learn to
skip — it would mask the drift that actually matters, this server moving to
another *jurisdiction*.

An earlier draft of this table asserted Postgres sat in the declared region. It
was caught by checking the running deployment rather than the IaC.

### The assertions that catch drift

The Azure stack shares a Container Apps environment, declared as a `data` source —
so its region is set by whoever created it, and **every Container App and Job in
the stack inherits it** (a Job must sit in its environment's region). Left
unchecked, moving or recreating that shared environment elsewhere would relocate
all of the app's compute with a clean `apply` and no signal.

`aca.tf` therefore carries a `postcondition` comparing the shared environment's
actual location against `var.azure_location`, so a mismatch **fails the plan**
with a message naming both. For a Ch. V control, "we did not notice the

The shared **database** gets the same comparison as a `check` block, which
**warns** rather than blocking. A `postcondition` there would fail every apply

decision, not a rollback.

It compares against `shared_pg_expected_location`, which defaults to
`azure_location` — so for an ordinary single-region deployment the two are the
same thing and the check is silent. Setting the variable is how a deployment

above. That indirection is the difference between a check that still works and
one that warns on every plan forever: an accepted exception must not cost you the
detector, and it must not hand the noise to every other deployment either.

1. **Concrete infrastructure identifiers of OUR estate**: resource group names (dataq-rg), Container App names (dataq-app-api, dataq-harness-*), Key Vault names/URLs, Azure subscription details, specific regions (West US 2/3, us-east-2, westus3), AWS account IDs, S3 bucket names (dataq-landing-*), CloudFront domains (d29cc3r7frs6eb.cloudfront.net), Databricks workspace URLs (dbc-*), Snowflake account identifiers (PVQSOEQ-*), warehouse/database/schema/role names specific to our harness (DATAQ_DB, DATAQ_WH, DATAQ_READER, DATAQ_LOADER, RETAIL, dataq_retail), demo user names/emails (Olivia, royarijit*), specific image tags (:v7, :v10), GitHub Actions run IDs/URLs, specific commit SHAs.

4. **Over-long / bloated passages**: places where a published page spends many paragraphs on narrative, history ("an earlier draft said X"), incident retrospectives, or internal decision-archaeology that a customer reading product documentation does not need. Note the file, approximate line range, and roughly how much could be cut. Be specific about WHICH passages are bloat vs. which length is warranted (a security page explaining a control genuinely needs detail).

For each finding report: file path, line number(s), the offending text (short quote), which category (1-4), and a one-line suggested fix. Do NOT edit any files — report only.

p = "deploy/terraform/azure/variables.tf"
s = open(p).read()
old = """# The region the shared PostgreSQL server is EXPECTED to be in.
#
# **Defaults to null, meaning "wherever azure_location says".** That is the
# correct expectation for any ordinary deployment — one region, everything in it —
# and it means the `check` in postgres.tf stays silent for them.
#
# THIS deployment overrides it, because it carries an accepted exception (#1465,
# G4/#434): the subscription caps Flexible Servers at one, so the app shares the
# harness's server, which sits in West US 3 while the app is in West US 2. Both
# are the same JURISDICTION (United States), which is what GDPR Ch. V keys on, so
# it is a region split rather than a residency problem — accepted deliberately
# rather than resolved, since resolving it means a new server plus a data
# migration against that same cap. The override lives in this deployment's
# tfvars, which is where a deployment-specific fact belongs.
#
# **Declared as a variable rather than left as prose, so the `check` keeps
# working.** Comparing the server against `azure_location` unconditionally would
# warn on EVERY plan here, and a permanently-firing check is noise people learn to
# skip — it would mask the drift that actually matters (this server moving to
# another *jurisdiction*). Baking "West US 3" in as the DEFAULT would have moved
# that same noise onto every other deployment instead, with a factually wrong
# warning attached.
"""
new = """# The region the shared PostgreSQL server is EXPECTED to be in (G4/#434).
#
# Null means "wherever azure_location says" — right for any ordinary deployment,
# and it keeps the `check` in postgres.tf silent. Set it only where the app is
# attached to a server someone else created, in a region this stack does not
# choose; that makes the mismatch a recorded decision instead of unexplained drift.
#
# A variable rather than prose, and null rather than a baked-in region, because
# both alternatives break the detector: comparing against `azure_location`
# unconditionally would warn on every plan of an exception-carrying deployment, and
# a hard-coded default would hand that same permanently-firing warning to everyone
# else. A check people learn to skip masks the drift that matters — the server
# moving to another *jurisdiction*, which is the unit GDPR Ch. V keys on.
#
# The value itself belongs in a deployment's own tfvars, not in this repo.
"""
assert old in s
s = s.replace(old, new, 1)
open(p, "w").write(s)

# aca.tf: drop the stale hardcoded "(westus2)"
p = "deploy/terraform/azure/aca.tf"
s = open(p).read()
old = """# separate, dataq-app-* resources. The env lives in azure_location (westus2), so
# the app's container resources land there too."""
new = """# separate, dataq-app-* resources. The env's own region is what the app's container
# resources inherit — which is what the residency assertion below is guarding."""
assert old in s
open(p, "w").write(s.replace(old, new, 1))
print("ok")

content.text:
Review findings fixed and pushed. The broader sweep you asked for is running across all published docs — I'll report when it lands.

Meanwhile, here's where the specific case ended up, since it turned out to be deeper than one table.

## The principle you named was right, and the repo settles it

`docs/security.md` **is published** to the public site; `docs/compliance-posture.md` is in `exclude_docs`. So our demo's regions were being published as the product's posture.

**Your instinct is backed by our own incident.** #1465 happened exactly this way — the matrix asserted Postgres sat in the declared region and it hadn't for some time. Nobody lied; the page was written once and the infrastructure moved. That's the failure mode of publishing live-infrastructure facts, and the fix isn't to re-check more often, it's to stop publishing them.

The published page now carries the **mechanism** (declare a region → `postcondition` blocks, `check` warns, `shared_pg_expected_location` records an exception) and points at `GET /api/v1/admin/deployment` for **values**, read live from the reader's own system. A control you can query beats a paragraph you have to trust.

## It went one layer deeper than docs

`postgres.tf` had `West US 3 / West US 2` hardcoded in a **tracked source comment** — the same defect, in code. Fixed; the value lives only in the gitignored tfvars, so the check still works locally.

## What I kept concrete, and why

CloudFront's global edge and the WAF's forced `us-east-1`. Those aren't our hosting — they're true of every AWS deployment, and a reviewer finding a `us-east-1` alias in an `eu-west` stack should find it explained.

## Review caught me inventing a control

I'd written that a shared **Container Apps environment** in another region can be declared via `shared_pg_expected_location`. It can't — that variable only feeds the Postgres check; the CAE postcondition has no override and hard-fails. Now stated as the deliberate asymmetry it is: one out-of-region database is a single resource; the CAE's region is inherited by *every* app and job, so accepting a mismatch there relocates the whole deployment.

Also fixed **four dead links** on the public site (published pages linking to `exclude_docs` files) — `mkdocs --strict` now reports zero.

## Audit: deployment-specific facts in PUBLISHED DataQ docs

**Critical framing point first:** `mkdocs.yml` `exclude_docs` lists 7 files, but **two more internal files sit in `docs/` and are neither excluded nor in `nav` — mkdocs still builds and publishes them** (nav omission does not exclude a page; it just isn't linked, and it *is* reachable by URL and indexed by the built-in search plugin):

- `/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/docs/ops-log.md` (529 lines)
- `/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/docs/post-v1-assets-lineage-incidents-notes.md` (164 lines)

That single omission is the largest finding in the audit, and everything in section A below flows from it.

---

## SEVERITY 1 — actively misleading / should never have been published

### A. `docs/ops-log.md` — the entire file (cat 1, 2, 4). Fix: add to `exclude_docs`.

This is a maintainer's private ops journal published verbatim on a public product site. It is 100% our-estate, contains a personal identity, an operational-security narrative, and cost data. Not fixable by editing; it should be excluded wholesale.

| Line | Quote | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 93 | `royarijit04@outlook.com` | Cat 1 — personal email as an actor column. Also lines 213, 335 `SHOW GRANTS TO USER ROYARIJIT04` (Snowflake username). |
| 78–92, 526–529 | `dataq-harness-airflow`, `dataq-harness-airflow-worker`, `dataq-harness-*`, `dataq-app-api`, `dataq-app-worker`, `dataq-rg` | Cat 1 — our Container App / RG names. |
| 89 | `Shared Postgres` **`dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd`** … reset the server's `airflowadmin` password … `DataQ prod uses the separate dataq_app role` | Cat 1, highest — a live server hostname fragment, admin role names, and the fact prod shares it. Reads as an attack map. |
| 83 | "an Airflow admin credential was briefly written to two scratch files via `terraform output` redirection (violates the inline-fetch-only rule) — caught immediately" | Cat 1/4 — a published self-report of a credential-handling incident on our infra. |
| 71, 79, 92, 527 | "the harness is burning ~CAD 17/day", "Extra burn ≈ CAD 4–5", "killed mid-poll by the account's monthly spend limit" | Cat 1 — our billing. |
| 80, 83 | "two messages purporting to be from 'a coordinator' arrived… Neither was acted on"; "I passively waited… roughly an hour… pure wasted awake-time cost" | Cat 4 — agent-session post-mortems on a product docs site. |
| 84 | `f637a18e`, revisions `--0000066` / `--0000064`, `plan -detailed-exitcode` | Cat 1 — commit SHA + revision numbers. |
| 143–481 | Six "Finding" sections (~340 lines) on our Snowflake grants, `DATAQ_LOADER`/`DATAQ_READER` PATs, `CREATE TAG` grants, an emulator spike, OpenTofu lock regeneration | Cat 1+4 — pure internal decision-archaeology. |
| 482–529 | "Credential rotation" / "Expiring soon" tables | Cat 1 — a public inventory of which of our secrets expire when. |

**Fix:** add `ops-log.md` to `exclude_docs`. Nothing here is product documentation.

### B. `docs/post-v1-assets-lineage-incidents-notes.md` — publish status inconsistent (cat 2/3)

Line 1–12: `> **Status: design for the next cycle's build (the #596 deliverable — no code in this PR)**`, links to `context/post-v1-roadmap.md`, "Themes 2/3/5/14". Line 76: `Harness test bed already green-on-paper: 4 RETAIL sources → 4 ANALYTICS_STG`. Its two sibling files (`post-v1-admin-ui-notes.md`, `post-v1-dq-intelligence-notes.md`) *are* excluded — this one was missed.
**Fix:** add to `exclude_docs`.

### C. `docs/adr/0028-cloud-neutral-image-runtime-config-generic-oidc.md:105-106` (cat 1)

```
az containerapp auth update -n dataq-app-api -g dataq-rg --enabled false
```
A copy-pasteable command naming **our** app and **our** resource group, presented as a migration step. A customer running it either errors or, worse, believes those are the product's required names.
**Fix:** `-n <your-api-app> -g <your-resource-group>`.

### D. `docs/deployment-parity.md:6` — broken ADR link (cat 3-adjacent, renders 404)

`.../docs/adr/0028-cloud-neutral-frontend-and-auth.md` — no such file; the real one is `0028-cloud-neutral-image-runtime-config-generic-oidc.md`. Also note this is an absolute GitHub URL where the in-site relative link `adr/0028-….md` would work.
**Fix:** correct the slug and make it a relative in-site link.

### E. `docs/security.md:276-300` — CMK "not offered, and why" (cat 1, misleading)

Two of the three stated reasons are facts about **our** subscription, published as if they were product limitations:
- L289: "`postgres.tf` declares it as a `data` source — **the subscription caps Flexible Servers at one**, so the app shares a server" — a free/trial-tier quota on *our* account.
- L294-296: "**Our** Key Vault is deliberately destroyable… purge protection **off**… a recorded decision for a **demo-scoped vault**."

A customer reads "DataQ does not support CMK." The truth is "our demo vault can't host a CMK." Reason 1 (creation-time-only, first-party citation) is the genuinely product-relevant one and should stay.
**Fix:** keep reason 1; recast 2 & 3 as "if your stack references a pre-existing server, or runs the vault without purge protection, CMK is unavailable — see [prerequisites]". Cuts ~20 lines and removes the false product claim.

### F. `docs/orchestration.md:208-212` (cat 1/2, will confuse and already rots)

> "**Not yet verified against a deployed app.** The Azure subscription lapsed (2026-07-12), so there is no running prod to attach a catalog to, and the harness Flow-A chain needs live Snowflake."

Our billing status published as a product caveat. Also L256 "live-verified on **the demo account** (RETAIL→STG→ANALYTICS chain)", L282 "captured from the live demo account/workspace (2026-07-17 spike)", L131-132 `DATAQ_DB.ANALYTICS.mart_order_revenue`.
**Fix:** "Verified locally and against captured payloads; not yet exercised against a deployed catalog." Drop the subscription sentence entirely; genericize the identifiers to `<db>.<schema>.<table>`.

### G. `docs/runbook-faq.md:24-29` (cat 1/2, stale-on-arrival)

> "**Snowflake window update (2026-07-04):** the trial runs to **~2026-07-25** (same as Azure). The #588 retirement was rehearsed and reversed the same day — the leg is live again on a fresh 25-day PAT (schedules/bindings restore pending, see #588)"

Entirely our trial account, with issue numbers a reader cannot open meaningfully, and a date already 13 months past. Also L20 heading "Live smoke (deployed stack + **harness** data)" and L40/42 "a **harness** suite", "a **harness** pipeline" — "the harness" is undefined for any reader.
**Fix:** delete the whole admonition; replace "harness" with "a suite backed by a real datasource" / "an orchestrated pipeline".

---

## SEVERITY 2 — will rot silently as our infra changes

### H. `docs/perf-baseline.md` (cat 1 + 2), several places

| Line | Quote | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 3-4 | "Captured 2026-07-10 (**v1.1 W3**), while both the Snowflake trial and the **Azure subscription were still live**" | Our billing + internal week numbering. |
| 36 | `App code | main @ e6b63fe1 (v1.1 W3)` | Commit SHA + week number. |
| 46-47 | `DATAQ_DB.PERF.ORDER_LINES_50M`, `dataq_retail.perf.order_lines_1m` | Our warehouse objects. |
| 51 | "burned **~0.46 Snowflake credits**" | Our billing. |
| 150, 162, 218, 228 | "v1.1 W6", "the W3 campaign", "the W3 UC datum" | Week-numbered milestones. |
| 283-312 | Whole appendix: "days before the Snowflake subscription was to lapse (the lapse was later reversed)… `DATAQ_READER` role… `--seed 587`, **harness repo per ADR 0021**" | See bloat item N. |

**Fix:** keep the *numbers* (genuinely useful product data), strip the account narrative; replace `DATAQ_DB.PERF.…` with `<db>.<schema>.order_lines_50m`; replace "v1.1 W3" with the release version.

### I. `docs/feature-matrix.md:32, 54` (cat 1)

`Snowflake RETAIL.ORDERS_HEADER row_count=34680.0`, `dataq_retail.gold.feedback_sentiment row_count=180.0` / `(195 rows)`.
Legitimate purpose (evidence that a ✅ was earned by a real run), illegitimate specificity.
**Fix:** "verified against a live Snowflake table and a live Unity Catalog table" — drop the object names and row counts. L191 "the reference **harness** runs this" → "verified against a self-hosted Airflow".

### J. `docs/deployment-parity.md` — framing (cat 2) and one over-specific row

The page is titled "How the **three reference installations** compare" — i.e. it documents *our* estate rather than the product. Most of the content is genuinely useful (the config-difference tables are exactly what an operator wants). The problems are the framing and two rows:
- L58-63 "## Test harness" table — "Full external harness (ADF pipelines, Airflow, dbt job; **opened on demand**)" / "**none**". Pure our-estate; means nothing to a customer.  **Fix: delete the section.**
- L39 rate-limiting cell — "live-verified 2026-08-16 — an unauthenticated burst through CloudFront allowed exactly the configured 120/min then 429'd…" This is ~4 lines of our test result in a comparison table. **Fix:** compress to "on (`RATE_LIMIT_XFF_TRUSTED_HOPS=3`)" and move the verification prose to `security.md` if it's worth keeping.
- L64-72 "AWS has a WAF ceiling and Azure has nothing equivalent… #1388" — accurate and useful as a *product* caveat, but phrased about our two stacks. **Fix:** reframe as "the Azure stack in this repo ships no WAF; add Front Door if you need edge limiting."

### K. `docs/deployment.md:167` (cat 1/2)

> "The **reference deployment** carries **demo/test fixtures** — tear them down before any customer-facing or marketplace use"

Reads as an instruction to the customer about *our* deployment, which they cannot act on. Otherwise `deployment.md` is clean and product-shaped — good baseline for the others.
**Fix:** "If you seeded demo fixtures (`scripts/setup.sh`), remove them before production use."

### L. ADR bare references to excluded pages (cat 2/3)

These are code-span mentions, not markdown links, so they don't render 404s — but they point a public reader at a page that does not exist on the site:
- `docs/adr/0012-monitor-kind-seam.md:177` — `` `docs/progress-v1.md` — Week 3 "Monitor abstraction…" tasks``
- `docs/adr/0010-provider-agnostic-infrastructure-seams.md:59` — "tracked in `docs/progress-v1.md` (Week 2…, Week 7…)"
- `docs/adr/0011-extensibility-seams-for-deferred-integrations.md:62` — "(Week 5 generic dispatch, Week 6 `ResultPublisher` seam)"
- `docs/adr/0005-severity-tier-weights.md:118` — "Week 3 … Week 6 health"
- `docs/adr/0021-demo-test-data-environment-strategy.md:14` — "carried in CLAUDE.md §13 and `docs/progress-v1.md`"
- `docs/adr/0033-workspace-roles-rbac.md:44` — "carried into `docs/security.md` / **`docs/compliance-posture.md`** by #742"
- `docs/adr/0024-app-deployment-infrastructure.md:159` — "the `docs/compliance-posture.md` evidence links"

**Fix:** drop the trailing "tracked in docs/progress-v1.md" lines from ADRs (they are the ADR's own build-tracking residue), and drop the `compliance-posture.md` mentions.

### M. `docs/adr/0024-app-deployment-infrastructure.md` — our estate, top to bottom (cat 1)

~30 hits across 250 lines: `dataq-rg`, `dataq-app-api`, `dataq-app-worker`, `dataq-app-migrate`, `dataq-cae`, `dataq-harness-*`, `dataq-harness-logs`, `dataq-app-ai`, `dataq-github-deploy`, "this **subscription** is hard-capped at one Container App Environment (`MaxNumberOfGlobalEnvironmentsInSubExceeded` — a **free/trial-tier** limit)", "the env's region is fixed (**westus2**)".

This is the hardest call in the audit. ADRs are decision records and naming the actual resources is what makes a decision record honest — I would **not** strip an ADR into genericity. But two things here are worse than the rest:
- The "free/trial-tier subscription cap" is presented as the *architectural reason* the app shares an environment with a harness the reader has never heard of. content.text:
The sweep found something bigger than the residency table.

## The real finding: two internal docs were live on the public site

**Omitting a file from mkdocs `nav` does not unpublish it.** MkDocs builds every `.md` under `docs/` and serves it by URL, indexed by search. Only `exclude_docs` unpublishes. Two files fell through:

- **`docs/ops-log.md`** — the maintainer ops journal. I confirmed it live at `https://theurgicduke771.github.io/DataQ/ops-log/` returning **200**, carrying your **personal email**, the **Postgres server name** `dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd`, Container App and RG names, CAD/day billing figures, and a **credential-expiry calendar**.
- **`docs/post-v1-assets-lineage-incidents-notes.md`** — whose two sibling design notes were already excluded; this one was simply missed.

Both are now in `exclude_docs`, with the nav-is-not-exclusion trap documented above the list.

**One honest limit: this reduces discoverability, it does not remove exposure.** The repo is **public**, so `ops-log.md` is still readable on GitHub. That's a separate decision and yours to make — CLAUDE.md mandates the file be git-tracked, so I didn't touch it. If the personal email and server name matter, the options are scrubbing those fields, or moving the file out of the repo.

## What else went

| Removed | Was |
|---|---|
| `az containerapp auth update -n dataq-app-api -g dataq-rg` | A copy-pasteable command naming *our* app — a customer running it errors, or believes those names are required |
| CMK "reasons 2 & 3" | Our subscription quota and demo vault, published as **product** limitations. A customer reads "DataQ doesn't support CMK"; the truth is "our demo vault can't host one" |
| "The Azure subscription lapsed (2026-07-12)" | Our billing status as a product caveat |
| A Snowflake trial-window note | 13 months stale on arrival |
| Warehouse names, row counts, commit SHA, "v1.1 W3" | Evidence claims survive; only the specificity that rots is gone |

## What I deliberately kept

**ADRs 0021 and 0024 keep their real resource names** — a decision record that genericizes its subject stops being evidence of what was decided. They gained a scope note saying they describe the maintainers' estate, not a product requirement. ADR 0021 now also *defines* "the harness", a word other pages used without ever introducing.

Also kept: CloudFront's edge and the WAF's forced `us-east-1` — product structure, true for every AWS deployment.

## Trim

~110 lines: a perf appendix its own header calls superseded, a footnote narrating a bug's biography where a customer needs the capability, an ADR aside about an unrelated drift bug.

**Verified against the built site, not the sources** — the email, DB hostname, CloudFront domain, Databricks workspace, Snowflake account and warehouse roles all return zero hits. `mkdocs --strict` clean, zero dead links, `tofu validate` passes.

Earlier review findings on this PR are also fixed — including one where I'd documented an escape hatch that doesn't exist (`shared_pg_expected_location` doesn't cover the Container Apps environment; its postcondition has no override).
